source.title: Up from Slavery
source.attribution: Booker T. Washington, Up from Slavery, Standard Ebooks, public domain

cards.title: Do the humble task so well that no one can fault it
cards.body:
When Booker T. Washington reached Hampton Institute after a long journey, tired, penniless and travel-worn, the head teacher hesitated to admit him. Then she asked him to sweep a classroom. He swept it three times and dusted every surface four times, sensing his future depended on it. She couldn't find a speck of dirt, and he was admitted.

He later urged people to do a common thing in an uncommon way, so thoroughly that nobody could improve on it. A small job done with unusual care is often the clearest evidence of what someone will do with a bigger one.
cards.quote: In a degree I felt that my whole future life depended upon the thoroughness with which I cleaned that room, and I was determined to do it so well that no one could find any fault with the job.
cards.locator: XVI. Europe ¶26
cards.apply_it: Pick one routine task today and do it noticeably better than required, as if someone were judging your future on it.

quiz.question: How did Washington win his place at Hampton Institute?
options: By passing a written exam
By sweeping and dusting a classroom with great thoroughness
By paying his fees in advance
Through a letter of recommendation
quiz.explanation: He later called the sweeping of that room his 'college examination', and the teacher could not find a speck of dirt.

cards.title: Measure success by the obstacles you've overcome
cards.body:
Washington, born into slavery, wrote that success should be judged less by the position someone reaches than by the obstacles they overcame on the way. Two people at the same level may have travelled very different distances to get there.

He also saw that hard struggle builds a strength and confidence that a smooth path doesn't. This is a healthier yardstick than comparing yourself with people who started with more. It doesn't excuse the barriers anyone faces, but it gives you credit for the ground you've actually covered.
cards.quote: I have learned that success is to be measured not so much by the position that one has reached in life as by the obstacles which he has overcome while trying to succeed.
cards.locator: II. Boyhood Days ¶25
cards.apply_it: Write down three obstacles you've overcome to get where you are. Reread them the next time you compare yourself with someone else.

quiz.question: How did Washington think success should be measured?
options: By wealth
By job title
By the obstacles overcome while trying to succeed
By fame
quiz.explanation: He judged success less by the position reached than by the obstacles overcome along the way.

cards.title: When the third attempt fails, find a way to fund the fourth
cards.body:
At Tuskegee, Washington wanted students to make their own bricks for the school's new buildings. Brickmaking turned out to be far harder than he expected. The first kiln failed, then the second, then a third. Teachers urged him to give up, the students were discouraged, and he had no money left.

He pawned his watch for fifteen dollars, rallied the team and tried again. The fourth kiln worked. He never got the watch back and never regretted it. Projects often fail at the point where people stop trying, not where the idea stops being good.
cards.quote: I returned to Tuskegee, and, with the help of the fifteen dollars, rallied our rather demoralized and discouraged forces and began a fourth attempt to make bricks. This time, I am glad to say, we were successful.
cards.locator: X. A Harder Task Than Making Bricks… ¶10
cards.apply_it: Think of a project you've shelved after a couple of failures. What could you put on the line for one more, better-planned attempt?

quiz.question: What did Washington do after three brick kilns failed?
options: Pawned his watch to fund a fourth attempt
Closed the brickyard
Bought bricks from a supplier
Hired outside experts
quiz.explanation: With no money left, he pawned his watch for fifteen dollars, and the fourth kiln succeeded.

cards.title: Lead by picking up the axe yourself
cards.body:
In the early days at Tuskegee, Washington wanted students to clear land for crops. Many, some of them former schoolteachers, felt manual labour was beneath an educated person and held back. Instead of lecturing them, he took an axe every afternoon after classes and led the way into the woods himself.

Once they saw he wasn't ashamed to work, they joined in with more enthusiasm, and together they cleared about twenty acres. People follow what leaders do far more than what they say. A manager who handles the unglamorous jobs sets the standard better than any memo.
cards.quote: When they saw that I was not afraid or ashamed to work, they began to assist with more enthusiasm.
cards.locator: VIII. Teaching School in a Stable and a… ¶29
cards.apply_it: Identify an unglamorous task your team or household avoids. Do it yourself this week, without comment.

quiz.question: How did Washington get reluctant students to clear land?
options: He threatened to expel them
He paid them extra
He hired labourers instead
He led the work himself with an axe every afternoon
quiz.explanation: Seeing him work without shame changed their minds more than any argument could.

cards.title: Speak only when you have something worth saying
cards.body:
Washington became one of the most sought-after speakers of his day, yet he believed you wrong both yourself and your audience when you speak just for the sake of it. Only when you're convinced you have something that will help someone should you stand up, and then conviction matters more than polished technique.

His mentor, General Armstrong, gave him another rule: give them an idea for every word. In meetings, presentations and posts, the same test applies. Before speaking, ask what you want the listener to take away. If there's no clear answer, stay quiet or keep it short.
cards.quote: I do not believe that one should speak unless, deep down in his heart, he feels convinced that he has a message to deliver.
cards.locator: XV. The Secret of Success in Public Speaking ¶16
cards.apply_it: Before your next meeting or presentation, write in one sentence what you want people to take away. Cut anything that doesn't serve it.

quiz.question: What advice did General Armstrong give Washington about speaking?
options: Always speak for at least an hour
Give them an idea for every word
Memorise every line
Open with a joke
quiz.explanation: 'Give them an idea for every word' was the one piece of advice Washington remembered and tried to follow ever after.

cards.title: Treat a small first 'yes' as a chance to prove yourself
cards.body:
The first time the railroad magnate Collis Huntington gave to Tuskegee, it was two dollars. Washington didn't resent the small amount. He resolved to show, through concrete results, that the school deserved more. Over about a dozen years Huntington's gifts grew as the school's usefulness grew, until he gave fifty thousand dollars.

Washington insisted this was hard work, not luck. Whether it's a first client, a small order or a trial project, a modest start is an invitation. Deliver visibly, keep the relationship warm, and bigger trust tends to follow.
cards.quote: When Mr. Huntington gave me the first two dollars, I did not blame him for not giving me more, but made up my mind that I was going to convince him by tangible results that we were worthy of larger gifts.
cards.locator: XII. Raising Money ¶22
cards.apply_it: Think of a small opportunity you've been given recently. What one tangible result could you deliver to earn a bigger one?

quiz.question: How did Washington respond to Huntington's first gift of two dollars?
options: He returned it
He asked for more straight away
He set out to prove with results that the school deserved more
He complained about it
quiz.explanation: He didn't blame Huntington for giving little; he worked for years to show tangible results, and the gifts grew to fifty thousand dollars.

cards.title: Keep your word even after you're no longer bound by it
cards.body:
Washington tells of a formerly enslaved man from Virginia who, before emancipation, had agreed to buy his own freedom in yearly payments while working in Ohio. When the Emancipation Proclamation freed him, he still owed about three hundred dollars. Legally the debt was gone. Yet he walked most of the way back to Virginia and paid every dollar, with interest.

The arrangement itself grew out of an unjust system, which makes his choice more striking. He told Washington he could not enjoy his freedom until he had kept his promise. For him, his word was part of who he was, not something a change in the law could cancel.
cards.quote: he knew that he did not have to pay the debt, but that he had given his word to the master, and his word he had never broken.
cards.locator: I. A Slave Among Slaves ¶15
cards.apply_it: Think of a promise you made that nobody could now hold you to. Decide whether you'll keep it anyway, and act on that decision this week.

quiz.question: Why did the man walk back to Virginia to pay his former master?
options: A court ordered him to pay
He had given his word and had never broken it
He wanted to buy land there
He hoped to be hired again
quiz.explanation: Emancipation had cancelled the debt, but he said he could not enjoy his freedom until he had kept his promise.

cards.title: Don't go into debt to look like you have more
cards.body:
On his first day at school, young Booker noticed that every other boy had a hat or cap, and he had none. His mother had no money for a 'store hat', the fashionable thing at the time. Rather than borrow to buy one, she sewed two pieces of homespun cloth into a cap.

Washington later said he was proud that she refused to go into debt for what she couldn't pay for, or to pretend to be what she wasn't. He noted, without satisfaction, that some boys who had mocked him from under their store hats later ended up in prison or poor. Borrowing to keep up appearances buys a moment of approval at the cost of lasting freedom.
cards.quote: my mother had strength of character enough not to be led into the temptation of seeming to be that which she was not
cards.locator: II. Boyhood Days ¶16
cards.apply_it: Before your next purchase meant partly to impress others, ask: would I buy this if nobody could see it? If not, skip it or find a homemade alternative.

quiz.question: What did Washington's mother do when he needed a cap for school?
options: Bought a store hat on credit
Borrowed one from a neighbour
Sewed one from two pieces of homespun cloth
Told him he didn't need one
quiz.explanation: She refused to go into debt for a store hat and made him a cap instead, which he valued more than any hat he owned later.

cards.title: If your days are taken, learn at night
cards.body:
As a boy, Washington worked in a salt furnace and then a coal mine, often starting at four in the morning. When the first school for Black children opened nearby, his stepfather wouldn't let him stop working. So he arranged lessons with the teacher at night, sometimes walking miles to recite, sometimes finding his teacher knew little more than he did. He believed he learned more at night than the other children did by day.

The lesson is not that everyone should work exhausting hours, but that a lack of daytime opportunity need not end your education. Evening classes, early mornings and online courses still let working people keep growing.
cards.quote: the greater part of the education I secured in my boyhood was gathered through the night-school after my day's work was done.
cards.locator: II. Boyhood Days ¶21
cards.apply_it: Block one regular evening or early-morning hour this week for learning something you care about, and protect it like an appointment.

quiz.question: How did Washington get most of his boyhood education?
options: Through night lessons after his day's work
At a boarding school
From a private tutor his family hired
By attending day school full time
quiz.explanation: Work kept him from regular day school, so he gathered most of his early education at night.

cards.title: Without an inheritance, build a record others can be proud of
cards.body:
Born into slavery, Washington knew almost nothing of his ancestry. He didn't know his father's name or who his grandmother was. He observed that people with a proud family history can draw strength from it, but may also be tempted to lean on it instead of doing the work themselves.

He turned his lack of inheritance into a purpose: he would create the record himself, for his children to build on. Many people start with no family wealth, connections or well-known name. That gap can become a reason to begin a tradition rather than a reason to feel behind.
cards.quote: Years ago I resolved that because I had no ancestry myself I would leave a record of which my children would be proud, and which might encourage them to still higher effort.
cards.locator: II. Boyhood Days ¶18
cards.apply_it: Write one sentence describing the example you want to leave for the next generation in your family. Choose one action this week that fits it.

quiz.question: What did Washington resolve because he had no known ancestry?
options: To rely on wealthy patrons for status
To spend years tracing his family tree
To avoid having children
To leave a record his children would be proud of
quiz.explanation: Lacking an inherited name or fortune, he resolved to create a record that would encourage his children to aim even higher.

cards.title: Let a demanding boss teach you lasting standards
cards.body:
To escape the coal mine, the teenage Washington became houseboy to Viola Ruffner, a woman so strict that most boys quit within weeks. He was afraid of her at first. Then he understood what she wanted: everything clean, work done promptly and systematically, and absolute honesty. Nothing slipshod; every fence and door kept in repair.

She became one of his best friends, and her standards stayed with him for life. Decades later he still couldn't pass litter or a broken fence without wanting to fix it. A tough manager or teacher can be uncomfortable, but if their demands are fair, they may be giving you habits worth more than a pay rise.
cards.quote: the lessons that I learned in the home of Mrs. Ruffner were as valuable to me as any education I have ever gotten anywhere else.
cards.locator: III. The Struggle for an Education ¶6
cards.apply_it: Think of the most demanding person you work or study with. Write down one of their standards you could adopt as your own.

quiz.question: What did Washington say about the lessons he learned working for Mrs. Ruffner?
options: They put him off domestic work forever
They were as valuable as any education he got anywhere
They were mainly about cooking
They were too strict to be useful
quiz.explanation: He said her lessons in cleanliness, promptness and honesty were as valuable as any education he ever received.

cards.title: Start your library with whatever books you can find
cards.body:
While working for Mrs. Ruffner, Washington built his first library out of a packing crate. He knocked out one side, fitted it with shelves, and filled it with every kind of book he could lay his hands on. Most of his studying was done at night, sometimes alone, sometimes with someone he paid to teach him.

A home library doesn't need fine furniture or a big budget. A box of second-hand books, borrowed titles or free e-books is enough to signal to yourself, and to any children in the house, that reading matters. Collecting books and keeping them close is itself a commitment to learning.
cards.quote: I secured a dry-goods box, knocked out one side of it, put some shelves in it, and began putting into it every kind of book that I could get my hands upon
cards.locator: III. The Struggle for an Education ¶7
cards.apply_it: Set aside one shelf, box or folder this week as your 'library'. Add one book you've been meaning to read.

quiz.question: What did Washington use for his first library?
options: A room at Hampton Institute
A shelf in the local church
A dry-goods box fitted with shelves
A bookcase lent by his employer
quiz.explanation: He knocked one side out of a packing box, added shelves and proudly called it his library.

cards.title: Take any honest work that keeps you moving toward your goal
cards.body:
On his 500-mile journey to Hampton Institute, Washington ran out of money in Richmond. He walked the streets past midnight, then slept under a raised wooden sidewalk with his bag for a pillow. In the morning he saw a ship unloading pig iron and asked the captain if he could help in exchange for money for food.

The captain kept him on for several days. Washington went on sleeping under the sidewalk to save every cent until he had enough to finish the trip. When a plan stalls for lack of money, humble, temporary work can be the bridge. It isn't a detour from the goal; it's part of reaching it.
cards.quote: I was tired, I was hungry, I was everything but discouraged.
cards.locator: III. The Struggle for an Education ¶13
cards.apply_it: If a goal is stuck for lack of money, list three short-term jobs or gigs you could do now to move it forward.

quiz.question: How did Washington earn money when he was stranded in Richmond?
options: By helping unload pig iron from a ship
By begging on the streets
By selling his satchel
By giving reading lessons
quiz.explanation: He asked a ship's captain for work unloading pig iron and kept at it until he could pay his way to Hampton.

cards.title: Make your work so valuable that you become indispensable
cards.body:
Washington arrived at Hampton with fifty cents. Board cost ten dollars a month, part of it payable in cash, and tuition was far beyond him. Given a job as janitor, he set out to do it so well the school couldn't manage without him, working late into the night and rising at four to light the fires.

It worked: he was soon told his work would cover the full cost of his board. (A donor found by General Armstrong paid his tuition.) Whatever your role, aim to be the person whose absence would be noticed. That reputation becomes leverage when you need flexibility, a raise or a second chance.
cards.quote: I was determined from the first to make my work as janitor so valuable that my services would be indispensable.
cards.locator: III. The Struggle for an Education ¶32
cards.apply_it: Identify one problem at work or home that only gets solved when you step in. How could you make that contribution more reliable and visible?

quiz.question: What was the result of Washington's work as a janitor at Hampton?
options: He was made a teacher straight away
He earned enough to buy a house
It won him a scholarship abroad
It came to cover the full cost of his board
quiz.explanation: His work became so valuable that the school credited him with the full cost of his board.

cards.title: Seek out great people: they teach what books can't
cards.body:
At Hampton, Washington met General Samuel Armstrong, the school's founder, whom he called the noblest person he ever knew. He said that even if every building, classroom and teacher were removed, daily contact with Armstrong would have been a liberal education in itself.

Washington came to believe that schools should study people and things as well as books. Character, judgement and generosity are caught as much as taught, by watching how admirable people handle pressure, money, conflict and other people. Choosing who you spend time with is one of the most important learning decisions you make.
cards.quote: there is no education which one can get from books and costly apparatus that is equal to that which can be gotten from contact with great men and women.
cards.locator: III. The Struggle for an Education ¶24
cards.apply_it: Name one person you admire for their character. Find a way this month to spend time with them, help them, or study how they work.

quiz.question: What did Washington say was worth more than education from books and costly equipment?
options: Travelling abroad
Contact with great men and women
Learning Latin and Greek
Winning debating contests
quiz.explanation: He believed nothing taught as much as direct contact with people of great character, like General Armstrong.

cards.title: Treat debts as debts of honour, and be frank when you can't pay
cards.body:
After his first year at Hampton, Washington owed the school sixteen dollars he hadn't been able to work off. All summer he saved toward it, doing his own washing and going without clothes he needed. Near the end he found a ten-dollar bill under a restaurant table, showed it to the owner, and watched him keep it.

Still short, he went to the school's treasurer and told him plainly where he stood. The treasurer let him return and trusted him to pay when he could. Taking debts seriously, and being honest early when you can't meet them, preserves the trust that makes people willing to give you more time.
cards.quote: I felt that this was a debt of honour, and that I could hardly bring myself to the point of even trying to enter school again till it was paid.
cards.locator: IV. Helping Others ¶5
cards.apply_it: If you owe someone and are falling behind, contact them this week with an honest update and a realistic plan.

quiz.question: What did Washington do when he still couldn't pay his sixteen-dollar debt?
options: Stayed away from school until he could pay
Asked a classmate to pay it
Told the school treasurer frankly about his situation
Kept the ten-dollar bill he found
quiz.explanation: He went to the treasurer, explained his condition honestly, and was trusted to pay the debt later.

cards.title: Begin every task expecting that you can succeed
cards.body:
After losing a found ten-dollar bill to a restaurant owner, Washington took stock. Looking back over his life, he wrote, he could not remember ever becoming discouraged about anything he set out to do. He began everything assuming he could succeed, and had little patience for people who are always ready to explain why something can't be done.

This isn't a promise that confidence guarantees results; Washington failed often, as his collapsed brick kilns show. But starting with the expectation of success keeps you looking for solutions rather than reasons to quit. Notice whose voices, including your own, mostly supply excuses.
cards.quote: I have begun everything with the idea that I could succeed, and I never had much patience with the multitudes of people who are always ready to explain why one cannot succeed.
cards.locator: IV. Helping Others ¶6
cards.apply_it: Pick one goal you've been doubting. Write three ways it could work before you allow yourself to list a single reason it can't.

quiz.question: How did Washington say he began everything he undertook?
options: With the idea that he could succeed
By listing every possible risk first
By waiting for others to approve
By lowering his expectations
quiz.explanation: He started each undertaking expecting to succeed and had little patience with people who explain why things can't be done.

cards.title: The happiest people are those who do the most for others
cards.body:
In his second year at Hampton, Washington was struck by his teachers' unselfishness. Many had left comfortable lives in the North to teach freed people, and they seemed happiest when helping students. At first he found it hard to understand. Then he came to see it as a rule of life.

He repeated it decades later: in meeting people everywhere, he found the happiest were those who did the most for others, and the most miserable those who did the least. It's a claim you can test in your own life. Notice how you feel after helping someone compared with a day spent only on yourself.
cards.quote: I think I began learning that those who are happiest are those who do the most for others.
cards.locator: IV. Helping Others ¶7
cards.apply_it: Do one unrequested helpful thing for someone today, then notice how you feel afterwards.

quiz.question: What lesson did Washington learn from his teachers at Hampton?
options: Teachers deserve more pay than others
Happiness comes mainly from wealth
Talent matters more than effort
Those who are happiest do the most for others
quiz.explanation: Watching his teachers' unselfishness, he concluded that the happiest people are those who do the most for others.

cards.title: Start the day with a few quiet minutes of meaningful reading
cards.body:
At Hampton, a teacher named Nathalie Lord taught Washington to use and love the Bible, both for its spiritual help and as literature. It became a lifelong habit: however busy he was, when at home he read a chapter or part of one each morning before starting the day's work.

For Washington this was an act of faith. Whatever your beliefs, the habit is worth borrowing. A short, unhurried reading before the phone, email and demands of the day can steady your mind and remind you what you care about. Keep it small enough that a busy day can't crowd it out.
cards.quote: no matter how busy I am, I always make it a rule to read a chapter or a portion of a chapter in the morning, before beginning the work of the day.
cards.locator: IV. Helping Others ¶9
cards.apply_it: Tomorrow morning, read one page or chapter of something that nourishes you before you check any messages.

quiz.question: What morning habit did Washington keep when he was at home?
options: Running before sunrise
Reading part of a chapter of the Bible before work
Writing letters to donors
Reading newspapers in bed
quiz.explanation: No matter how busy he was, he read a chapter or part of one each morning before starting work.

cards.title: Turn idle minutes into practice time
cards.body:
At Hampton, Washington noticed that between supper and evening study there were about twenty minutes the young men usually spent in idle gossip. He and about twenty others formed a society to use that gap for debate and public-speaking practice.

Washington went on to become one of the most famous speakers of his time. Small, regular windows add up: twenty minutes a day is over a hundred hours a year. Look for the predictable gaps in your day, the commute, the wait before a meeting, the time after dinner, and give a few of them a purpose.
cards.quote: Few persons ever derived more happiness or benefit from the use of twenty minutes of time than we did in this way.
cards.locator: IV. Helping Others ¶11
cards.apply_it: Find one 15–20 minute gap you usually waste. Assign it to one skill you want to build, and try it for a week.

quiz.question: How did Washington's group use the twenty minutes after supper at Hampton?
options: For extra sleep
For cleaning the dormitories
For debate and public-speaking practice
For writing letters home
quiz.explanation: They turned twenty minutes of idle gossip into regular practice in debate and public speaking.

cards.title: No honest work is beneath you
cards.body:
Before Hampton, Washington shared a common belief of the time: that getting an education meant escaping manual work. Hampton changed his mind. He watched Mary Mackie, the head teacher, from one of the North's most cultured families, spend two weeks beside him cleaning windows, dusting and making beds before term began, and take real satisfaction in it.

He came to love work not only for its pay but for the independence and self-reliance that come from being able to do something the world wants done. In many places today, educated people still treat hands-on work as low. Respecting all useful work widens your options and earns the respect of those who do it.
cards.quote: At Hampton I not only learned that it was not a disgrace to labour, but learned to love labour
cards.locator: IV. Helping Others ¶24
cards.apply_it: Thank someone whose practical work makes your day easier, and ask them to teach you one skill they use.

quiz.question: What did head teacher Mary Mackie do before each school year at Hampton?
options: Cleaned windows and rooms alongside Washington
Hired extra servants
Took a long holiday
Raised money in the North
quiz.explanation: Despite her education and social standing, she worked beside him cleaning the buildings, which taught him the dignity of labour.

cards.title: Lift up the people who lifted you
cards.body:
While Washington studied at Hampton, his older brother John worked in the coal mines to support the family and sent him what he could. Washington never forgot it. Once he was teaching, he helped prepare John for Hampton and saved to help with his expenses. John graduated and later ran the industries at Tuskegee. Together the brothers then put their adopted brother James through Hampton too.

In many families, one person sacrifices so another can study or get started. Success brings a quiet debt to those who carried you, and repaying it by opening the same door for them multiplies what was given.
cards.quote: He willingly neglected his own education that he might help me.
cards.locator: IV. Helping Others ¶30
cards.apply_it: Think of someone who sacrificed so you could get ahead. What is one concrete way you could help them, or their children, this year?

quiz.question: How did Washington repay his brother John's sacrifice?
options: He paid for John to retire early
He found John a job in politics
He gave John his share of the family land
He helped John prepare for and attend Hampton
quiz.explanation: Once working, Washington helped John get to Hampton; John later became Superintendent of Industries at Tuskegee.

cards.title: Live on what you earn, not on what you want people to think
cards.body:
Studying in Washington, DC, in his twenties, Washington was alarmed by the superficial living he saw among some young men. Some earning four dollars a week spent half of it hiring a carriage for a Sunday drive, to look wealthy. Others on good government salaries were in debt by the end of every month.

The problem he saw wasn't enjoyment but spending to impress. Status spending is a treadmill: it costs real money, buys an illusion and leaves you less able to build anything. Whatever your income, the person who looks rich and the person who is building wealth are often not the same person.
cards.quote: I saw young coloured men who were not earning more than four dollars a week spend two dollars or more for a buggy on Sunday to ride up and down Pennsylvania Avenue in
cards.locator: V. The Reconstruction Period ¶13
cards.apply_it: Review last month's spending. Circle anything bought mainly to be seen, and move that amount into savings this month.

quiz.question: What did some young men earning four dollars a week spend half their pay on?
options: Night-school fees
Hiring a buggy for a Sunday drive to look wealthy
Books and newspapers
Money sent home to their parents
quiz.explanation: Washington saw them spend two dollars of a four-dollar wage to convince the world they were rich.

cards.title: Choose work that lasts over success that only serves you
cards.body:
After a successful speaking campaign in West Virginia, people urged the young Washington to go into politics. He believed he could have succeeded. But he felt it would be a selfish kind of success: a personal career won while neglecting the work he thought his people most needed, a foundation in education, skills and property.

He chose teaching instead, and later built Tuskegee. Most of us face smaller versions of this choice: the visible, rewarding path versus the slower one that builds something for others. There's no rule that the first is wrong, but it's worth asking which you'll be glad you chose.
cards.quote: As for my individual self, it appeared to me to be reasonably certain that I could succeed in political life, but I had a feeling that it would be a rather selfish kind of success
cards.locator: VI. Black Race and Red Race ¶2
cards.apply_it: Write down two paths open to you now. For each, ask: who besides me will benefit from this in ten years?

quiz.question: Why did Washington turn down a political career?
options: He was told he lacked speaking skills
He was too young to vote
He felt it would be a selfish success compared with building foundations for his people
He had already run for office and lost
quiz.explanation: He believed he could succeed in politics but chose work he thought would be of more lasting value to his race.

cards.title: No one can degrade you unless you let them
cards.body:
Washington recalls a story told by Frederick Douglass. Forced by racial rules to ride in a train's baggage car though he had paid full fare, Douglass was visited by white passengers who said they were sorry he'd been degraded. He replied that they could not degrade Frederick Douglass: it was those inflicting the treatment who were degraded, not him.

This isn't a reason to accept injustice; Douglass spent his life fighting it. It's about where your dignity lives. Insults, discrimination and humiliation are real harms, yet your worth is not in the hands of those who mistreat you.
cards.quote: The soul that is within me no man can degrade.
cards.locator: VI. Black Race and Red Race ¶14
cards.apply_it: Recall a time someone treated you with contempt. Write one sentence about what that behaviour revealed about them, not about you.

quiz.question: According to Douglass, who was degraded when he was forced into the baggage car?
options: Those inflicting the treatment on him
Douglass himself
Only the railway company
Nobody, since it was the law
quiz.explanation: Douglass said no one could degrade the soul within him; the shame belonged to those who mistreated him.

cards.title: Judge character by how people treat those with less power
cards.body:
Washington believed the real test of a gentleman is how he behaves toward people less fortunate than himself. He told a story about George Washington, who once returned the polite hat-lift of a Black man he met on the road. When friends criticised him, the first president said he would not let anyone be more polite than he was.

The principle reaches beyond race. How someone treats a waiter, cleaner, junior colleague or stranger who can do nothing for them reveals more than how they treat the powerful. It's a good test for choosing friends, partners and employers, and for checking ourselves.
cards.quote: My experience has been that the time to test a true gentleman is to observe him when he is in contact with individuals of a race that is less fortunate than his own.
cards.locator: VI. Black Race and Red Race ¶17
cards.apply_it: Next time you meet someone who can do nothing for you, greet them with the same courtesy you'd give your boss.

quiz.question: When did Washington say a true gentleman is best tested?
options: When speaking to a large audience
When he is among close friends
When he is under financial pressure
When dealing with people less fortunate than himself
quiz.explanation: He believed character shows most clearly in how we treat those with less power or fortune than ourselves.

cards.title: Go and see real conditions before you make your plan
cards.body:
Before opening the Tuskegee school, Washington spent his first month travelling Alabama's back roads by mule and cart. He ate and slept in people's cabins and saw their farms, schools and churches. Because he usually arrived unannounced, he saw daily life as it really was rather than as people might present it to a visitor.

What he saw shaped everything: he concluded that copying book-only education from New England would not meet these families' needs. Whether you're starting a business, a project or a charity, firsthand observation of the people you hope to serve beats assumptions made from a distance.
cards.quote: I had the advantage of seeing the real, everyday life of the people.
cards.locator: VII. Early Days at Tuskegee ¶12
cards.apply_it: Before your next big decision about other people, spend time where they are: visit, listen and watch before proposing anything.

quiz.question: How did Washington spend his first month in Tuskegee?
options: Raising money in Boston
Travelling the countryside and staying in people's cabins
Building the first school hall
Writing the school's rules
quiz.explanation: He travelled unannounced through rural Alabama to see how people really lived before designing the school.

cards.title: Cover the basics before buying showpieces on credit
cards.body:
In the cabins around Tuskegee, Washington often found expensive sewing machines and showy clocks bought on instalments. At one family meal there was a single fork for five people, while in the corner stood an organ they were paying for in monthly instalments. Nobody in the family could play it, and the clocks often didn't keep time.

Hire purchase and buy-now-pay-later plans make big items feel affordable while everyday needs go unmet. Washington's 'one fork' test still works: before committing to monthly payments, ask whether the basics, food, tools, health and savings, are covered first.
cards.quote: In the opposite corner of that same cabin was an organ for which the people told me they were paying sixty dollars in monthly instalments. One fork, and a sixty-dollar organ!
cards.locator: VII. Early Days at Tuskegee ¶15
cards.apply_it: List any instalment payments you're making. For each, ask whether you'd buy it again today, and pause new ones until the basics are covered.

quiz.question: What did Washington find in a cabin where five people shared one fork?
options: A new bicycle
A large library of books
An organ being paid for in monthly instalments
A savings box full of coins
quiz.explanation: The family had one fork but was paying sixty dollars in instalments for an organ nobody could play.

cards.title: Master the basics before reaching for advanced topics
cards.body:
When Washington opened Tuskegee, many students arrived eager to show off big words and advanced subjects. One had been studying cube root and 'banking and discount' but could not handle simple arithmetic. Washington found the courage to tell him plainly that his first job was to master the multiplication table.

It is tempting to skip ahead to the impressive-sounding material, whether in maths, a trade or a new career. But advanced skills rest on fundamentals. Washington's point is that honest teaching, and honest self-assessment, start from where you really are, not from where you would like to appear to be.
cards.quote: the wisest thing for him to do first was thoroughly master the multiplication table.
cards.locator: VIII. Teaching School in a Stable and a… ¶12
cards.apply_it: Pick one skill you are trying to improve. List its three most basic building blocks and test yourself honestly on each one.

quiz.question: What did Washington tell the student who had been studying cube root?
options: To master the multiplication table first
To move straight on to algebra
To leave school and start a bank
To focus on Latin and Greek instead
quiz.explanation: The student had skipped the basics, so Washington advised him to go back and master the multiplication table before anything else.

cards.title: Treat your credit, your reputation for paying, as capital
cards.body:
In Tuskegee's early years, money was always short and bills kept arriving. George W. Campbell, the local man who had helped bring Washington to Tuskegee, gave him one piece of fatherly advice that he never forgot: credit is capital.

The idea is simple and still true. A record of paying what you owe, on time, is an asset that lets you borrow, buy stock or win contracts when cash is tight. Breaking promises to lenders and suppliers spends that capital quickly. For a small business or a household, protecting your name with creditors can matter as much as the money in the bank.
cards.quote: Washington, always remember that credit is capital.
cards.locator: IX. Anxious Days and Sleepless Nights ¶24
cards.apply_it: List every bill or debt you currently owe. Mark any that are at risk of being late, and contact that lender before the due date, not after.

quiz.question: What advice did George W. Campbell give Washington?
options: Never borrow money for any reason
Spend first and raise funds later
Keep the school small to avoid debts
Always remember that credit is capital
quiz.explanation: Campbell told him that credit is capital: a good record with lenders is a resource worth protecting.

cards.title: People protect what they helped build
cards.body:
At Tuskegee, students made the bricks and put up many of the buildings themselves. Washington noticed a side effect. When a new student was tempted to scratch or scribble on a wall, an older student would stop him, saying it was their building because they had helped put it up.

Washington had chosen student labour partly to teach skills and save money, but it also created a sense of ownership that no rule could. Teams, families and communities that share in the work tend to look after the result. If you want people to care about something, let them have a real hand in creating it.
cards.quote: Don't do that. That is our building. I helped put it up.
cards.locator: X. A Harder Task Than Making Bricks… ¶5
cards.apply_it: Think of a shared space or project you want others to care for. Find one real task they could help build or shape rather than just use.

quiz.question: Why did older Tuskegee students stop newcomers from marking the buildings?
options: They were paid as security guards
They had helped build them and felt they owned them
Damage was fined heavily by the school
The buildings were rented from the town
quiz.explanation: Having helped put the buildings up, the older students felt the buildings were theirs and protected them.

cards.title: Visible results persuade more than arguments
cards.body:
Washington observed that people tend to recognise and reward real merit, whatever the colour of the person who shows it. He believed that the visible, tangible result does more to soften prejudice than any amount of argument. A well-built house, he said, is far more convincing than pages of discussion about a house someone could build.

This does not mean injustice should go unchallenged, and Washington's wider approach to civil rights is still debated. But as a working principle it holds: when you want to change minds about your ability, a finished product, a working prototype or a satisfied customer often speaks louder than a speech.
cards.quote: The actual sight of a first-class house that a Negro has built is ten times more potent than pages of discussion about a house that he ought to build
cards.locator: X. A Harder Task Than Making Bricks… ¶14
cards.apply_it: Is there a claim about your ability you keep trying to argue? Decide what small, finished piece of work could demonstrate it instead.

quiz.question: According to Washington, what softens prejudice more than discussion?
options: Avoiding contact with critics
Newspaper debates
The visible, tangible result of good work
Keeping quiet about your achievements
quiz.explanation: He found that the actual sight of a first-class building was ten times more potent than pages of discussion.

cards.title: Do something the world needs and it will find a way to reward you
cards.body:
Washington argued that a person who can do something the world wants done will, in the end, make a way, even against prejudice. He gave an example: a community may have no use for someone offering Greek grammar, but it will gladly pay for bricks, houses and wagons. Meet that need first, he said, and the demand for the finer things will come later, along with the means to enjoy them.

For anyone choosing a trade or starting a business, the question is not only 'what do I like?' but 'what do the people around me need and lack?'. Being useful is a strong foundation for both income and respect.
cards.quote: The individual who can do something that the world wants done will, in the end, make his way regardless of race.
cards.locator: X. A Harder Task Than Making Bricks… ¶16
cards.apply_it: Ask three people in your community what service or product they struggle to find. Note whether any of these matches a skill you have or could learn.

quiz.question: In Washington's example, what would a community value before Greek analysis?
options: Bricks, houses and wagons
Poetry recitals
Lectures on philosophy
Imported luxury goods
quiz.explanation: He argued that meeting practical needs like bricks and houses comes first, and that demand for higher learning follows.

cards.title: Refuse to let anyone shrink your soul by making you hate them
cards.body:
Washington learned from General Samuel Armstrong, his teacher at Hampton, that hatred harms the one who carries it. He resolved that no person, of any colour, would narrow and degrade his soul by making him hate them. He wrote that he pitied anyone caught in the habit of race prejudice.

This was not a denial that wrongs had been done; he lived through slavery and its aftermath. It was a decision about what he would allow those wrongs to do to him inside. Resentment can quietly take over a life. Choosing not to hate is a way of keeping your own mind free.
cards.quote: resolved that I would permit no man, no matter what his colour might be, to narrow and degrade my soul by making me hate him.
cards.locator: XI. Making Their Beds Before They Could Lie… ¶4
cards.apply_it: Think of someone you resent. Write down what that resentment costs you each week in energy or peace, and one step that would loosen its grip.

quiz.question: What did Washington resolve about people who wronged him or his race?
options: He would never speak to them again
He would publicly expose each one
He would move to the North to avoid them
He would not let them degrade his soul by making him hate them
quiz.explanation: Following Armstrong's example, he refused to let anyone make him hate them, because hatred narrows the soul.

cards.title: Give people responsibility and invite their honest criticism
cards.body:
Washington wanted Tuskegee students to feel the school was theirs, and to see him as a friend and adviser rather than an overseer. Two or three times a year he asked every student to write him a letter with complaints, criticism or suggestions, or held open meetings to talk frankly about how the school was run. He said no meetings helped him plan better.

He believed that trusting people with responsibility helps them grow, and suggested that many conflicts between employers and workers could be avoided if managers consulted their staff and showed that their interests were shared. Asking for honest feedback is a sign of strength, not weakness.
cards.quote: Few things help an individual more than to place responsibility upon him, and to let him know that you trust him.
cards.locator: XI. Making Their Beds Before They Could Lie… ¶14
cards.apply_it: Ask the people you lead, at work or at home, for one honest suggestion or complaint. Listen without defending yourself, then act on one point.

quiz.question: How often did Washington ask students to write him letters of criticism and suggestions?
options: Never; he preferred discipline
Two or three times a year
Only when a student was expelled
Once, when the school opened
quiz.explanation: Two or three times a year he invited written criticism or held frank meetings, and found them very helpful for planning.

cards.title: Do your full duty, then stop worrying about the outcome
cards.body:
Washington spent years raising money for Tuskegee, often with bills due and nothing in hand. Asked for his rules, he gave only two: do your whole duty in making the work known, and do not worry about the results. He admitted the second was the hardest.

He came to see worry as a waste: it uses up physical and mental strength that could go into useful work, without changing anything. The people he most admired stayed calm, patient and polite under pressure. Separating what you can do from what you can't control frees energy for the part that is yours.
cards.quote: all worry simply consumes, and to no purpose, just so much physical and mental strength that might otherwise be given to effective work.
cards.locator: XII. Raising Money ¶7
cards.apply_it: For a situation you're anxious about, write two lists: what I can still do, and what is out of my hands. Act on the first list today.

quiz.question: What were Washington's two rules for raising money?
options: Ask often, and ask only the richest
Promise big returns, then deliver later
Do your whole duty, and don't worry about the results
Never travel, and write many letters
quiz.explanation: He did his full duty in making the work known and tried not to worry, since worry wastes strength.

cards.title: Help others succeed without seeing it as your loss
cards.body:
When Tuskegee was desperate for funds, General Armstrong, head of Hampton Institute, invited Washington to tour the North with him and introduced him to Hampton's own donors. Washington noted that a narrow man would have seen every dollar given to Tuskegee as a dollar taken from Hampton. Armstrong saw it differently: both schools served the same larger cause, and helping a newer effort strengthened his own.

In business and community life, colleagues and similar organisations are often treated as rivals. Armstrong's example suggests that sharing contacts and opportunities can grow the whole field and build lasting goodwill.
cards.quote: He was too big to be little, too good to be mean.
cards.locator: XII. Raising Money ¶4
cards.apply_it: Introduce someone whose work you respect to a contact, customer or opportunity that could help them, even if they work in your field.

quiz.question: Why did Armstrong introduce Washington to Hampton's Northern supporters?
options: He saw both schools serving one larger cause
He wanted to close Hampton
Washington paid him a commission
He was ordered to by the government
quiz.explanation: A narrow man would have seen Tuskegee's gains as Hampton's loss; Armstrong saw a shared cause and helped.

cards.title: Effort that seems wasted may pay off years later
cards.body:
Washington once walked two miles through a cold storm outside Stamford, Connecticut, to explain Tuskegee's needs to a man he had heard might help. After three hours the man gave nothing, and Washington felt the day had been thrown away. Still, he had done his duty.

Two years later a letter arrived with ten thousand dollars. The man had put the sum in his will but decided to give it while he was alive, and he mentioned the visit. Not every meeting brings an immediate result. Doing your part well, and leaving a good impression, can bear fruit long after you've stopped expecting it.
cards.quote: I had placed this sum in my will for your school, but deem it wiser to give it to you while I live. I recall with pleasure your visit to me two years ago.
cards.locator: XII. Raising Money ¶17
cards.apply_it: Recall a pitch, application or meeting that seemed to go nowhere. Send a short, friendly follow-up or update to keep the door open.

quiz.question: What happened two years after the visit in which the Stamford man gave nothing?
options: He wrote to complain about the visit
He asked Washington to repay his time
He joined the school as a teacher
He sent ten thousand dollars
quiz.explanation: He sent a draft for ten thousand dollars, saying he recalled the visit with pleasure.

cards.title: You win people over by giving credit, not by abuse
cards.body:
Washington decided early to make Tuskegee his home and to speak about the South in the North exactly as he would in the South. He also learned that abusing people rarely changes their minds. People are more often won over when you give credit for the good they do than when you only point out the wrong.

This does not mean ignoring wrongdoing. It means that criticism lands better when the other person knows you also see their good side. At home, at work or in public life, recognising what people do well builds the trust that makes honest correction possible.
cards.quote: it is a hard matter to convert an individual by abusing him
cards.locator: XIII. Two Thousand Miles for a Five-Minute… ¶9
cards.apply_it: Before giving someone criticism this week, first tell them something specific they did well, and mean it.

quiz.question: What did Washington learn about changing people's minds?
options: Public shaming is the quickest method
Giving credit for good actions works better than abuse
Silence is always the best approach
Only legal pressure changes behaviour
quiz.explanation: He found that converting someone by abuse is hard; giving credit for praiseworthy actions works more often.

cards.title: Don't let your grievances hide your opportunities
cards.body:
In his 1895 Atlanta Exposition address, Washington urged Black Southerners to put skill and pride into farming, trades, commerce and the professions. He argued that there is as much dignity in tilling a field as in writing a poem, and that one must start at the bottom, not the top. Then he added: don't let grievances overshadow opportunities.

His wider political compromise in that speech was sharply criticised by contemporaries such as W. E. B. Du Bois, and the debate continues. The personal lesson is narrower: real wrongs deserve attention, but focusing only on them can blind you to the openings still within reach.
cards.quote: Nor should we permit our grievances to overshadow our opportunities.
cards.locator: XIV. The Atlanta Exposition Address ¶6
cards.apply_it: Write down one grievance that occupies your mind. Next to it, write one opportunity available to you right now that it may be hiding.

quiz.question: In the Atlanta address, what did Washington say should not overshadow opportunities?
options: Education
Religion
Grievances
Family duties
quiz.explanation: He said we should not permit our grievances to overshadow our opportunities, while urging dignity in common labour.

cards.title: When you're sure you're right and are condemned, stay calm and let time speak
cards.body:
Washington once wrote a magazine article criticising poorly trained ministers, and for about a year church bodies across the country denounced him. He didn't fight back. Over the years, standards among the clergy rose, and he wrote that ministers became some of his warmest friends.

From this he drew a rule: when you're confident you have said or done the right thing and are condemned for it, stand still and stay quiet. If you are right, time will show it. Answering every attack can drag you into endless quarrels. Patience lets the results argue for you, though it is worth first making sure you really are right.
cards.quote: the thing to do, when one feels sure that he has said or done the right thing, and is condemned, is to stand still and keep quiet. If he is right, time will show it.
cards.locator: XIV. The Atlanta Exposition Address ¶30
cards.apply_it: Next time you're criticised online or at work, wait 24 hours before replying. Ask whether a reply is needed at all, or whether results will answer for you.

quiz.question: What did Washington recommend when you're condemned for doing what you're sure is right?
options: Stand still, keep quiet and let time show it
Issue a public apology at once
Attack your critics' motives
Resign from your position
quiz.explanation: His experience with the ministers taught him that, if you are right, time will show it.

cards.title: Don't let a big offer pull you away from your real work
cards.body:
After the Atlanta speech made him famous, Washington was flooded with offers. One lecture bureau offered him fifty thousand dollars, or two hundred dollars a night plus expenses. He turned them all down. His life's work, he replied, was at Tuskegee, and he would only speak in the interest of the school and his people.

Sudden success often brings tempting offers that would quietly redirect your life. Some are worth taking. But Washington's example asks you to test them against your main purpose, and to refuse arrangements that put a mere price on work you believe matters for its own sake.
cards.quote: To all these communications I replied that my lifework was at Tuskegee; and that whenever I spoke it must be in the interests of Tuskegee school and my race
cards.locator: XIV. The Atlanta Exposition Address ¶18
cards.apply_it: Write one sentence that defines your main purpose this year. Use it as a filter the next time an offer or invitation arrives.

quiz.question: How did Washington respond to a lecture bureau's offer of fifty thousand dollars?
options: He accepted and gave the money to the school
He negotiated for a higher fee
He accepted for one year only
He declined, saying his lifework was at Tuskegee
quiz.explanation: He refused all such offers, saying he would only speak in the interests of Tuskegee and his race.

cards.title: Even experienced speakers feel nervous; speak anyway
cards.body:
By the time he wrote his autobiography, Washington had addressed huge audiences across America, including presidents. People assumed he no longer felt nerves. He admitted the opposite: before speaking he always suffered intense nervousness, sometimes so bad he vowed never to speak again. Afterwards he often regretted leaving out his best point.

This is encouraging for anyone who dreads presenting. Nervousness is not a sign that you're unfit for the task; it is a normal reaction even among the most accomplished. The skill lies in preparing well and going ahead despite the feeling, not in waiting for it to disappear.
cards.quote: I always suffer intensely from nervousness before speaking.
cards.locator: XV. The Secret of Success in Public Speaking ¶14
cards.apply_it: Before your next presentation or hard conversation, name the nervous feeling out loud or on paper, then prepare your first two sentences so you can start strong.

quiz.question: What did Washington say about feeling nervous before speeches?
options: He stopped feeling nervous after his first year
He always suffered intensely from nervousness
He never felt nervous at all
He only felt nervous in the South
quiz.explanation: Despite his experience, he wrote that he always suffered intense nervousness before speaking.

cards.title: Don't do what others can do as well
cards.body:
Washington ran a large and growing school while spending much of each year away raising funds. Asked how, he said he had learned to ignore the old saying that you shouldn't ask others to do what you can do yourself. His own motto was to avoid doing what others could do as well.

He built an organisation of department heads, an executive council and a finance committee, so the school ran like clockwork whether or not he was there. Delegation frees a leader to focus on the work only he or she can do. It also gives others the responsibility that helps them grow.
cards.quote: Do not do that which others can do as well.
cards.locator: XV. The Secret of Success in Public Speaking ¶45
cards.apply_it: List your regular tasks this week. Circle one that someone else could do as well as you, and hand it over with clear instructions.

quiz.question: Which motto did Washington adopt about work?
options: Do everything yourself to be sure it's right
Never ask for help from staff
Do not do that which others can do as well
Work only when inspired
quiz.explanation: He rejected the maxim about doing everything yourself and chose to delegate whatever others could do as well.

cards.title: Stay ahead of your work so it doesn't drive you
cards.body:
Washington described a daily method for handling a heavy workload. He planned each day, cleared routine tasks as early as possible, and then turned to new or forward-looking work. Before leaving the office, he cleared his desk of letters and notes so that each morning started fresh.

His aim was to master his work rather than be its servant. He said that staying ahead of it gave him a satisfying sense of control and helped keep him healthy and energetic. A clear end-of-day reset and doing routine tasks early are simple habits that still protect focus today.
cards.quote: I make it a rule never to let my work drive me, but to so master it, and keep it in such complete control, and to keep so far ahead of it, that I will be the master instead of the servant.
cards.locator: XV. The Secret of Success in Public Speaking ¶49
cards.apply_it: Spend the last ten minutes of today clearing your desk or inbox and writing tomorrow's first task, so you start the morning in control.

quiz.question: What did Washington do before leaving his office each day?
options: Cleared his desk of all correspondence and notes
Wrote a long diary entry
Held a staff meeting
Left tasks for the night guard
quiz.explanation: He cleared his desk daily so the next day could begin fresh, as part of mastering his work.

cards.title: Expect a good day, but prepare yourself for bad news
cards.body:
Washington began each morning expecting a successful and pleasant day. At the same time, he mentally prepared for trouble: a school building on fire, an accident, or someone attacking him in a speech or newspaper, perhaps over words he never said.

This combination is practical. Optimism gives energy, while quietly accepting that setbacks will come stops them from knocking you off balance. When a problem arrives, it feels like something you had already allowed for, not a disaster. You can then respond with a clear head.
cards.quote: When I begin my work in the morning, I expect to have a successful and pleasant day of it, but at the same time I prepare myself for unpleasant and unexpected hard places.
cards.locator: XV. The Secret of Success in Public Speaking ¶50
cards.apply_it: Each morning this week, name one thing you expect to go well and one possible setback, with how you'd calmly respond.

quiz.question: How did Washington start each working day?
options: Expecting the worst so nothing disappointed him
Ignoring possible problems completely
Reading every newspaper criticism first
Expecting success while preparing for hard places
quiz.explanation: He expected a successful, pleasant day but also prepared himself for unpleasant surprises.

cards.title: Look after small health problems before they grow
cards.body:
Washington believed everyone has a duty to keep the body in good condition, especially people carrying heavy responsibilities. His approach was to attend to small ills early, hoping to prevent bigger ones. If he couldn't sleep well, he took it as a sign something was wrong, and if any part of his body seemed weak he consulted a good doctor.

He also trained himself to take short naps of fifteen or twenty minutes and wake refreshed. The general lesson is sensible: notice early warning signs like poor sleep, and get proper medical advice rather than waiting for a crisis.
cards.quote: I try to look after the little ills, with the idea that if I take care of the little ills the big ones will not come.
cards.locator: XV. The Secret of Success in Public Speaking ¶51
cards.apply_it: Is there a small health niggle you've been ignoring? Book a check-up or make one simple change this week to address it.

quiz.question: What did Washington treat as a sign that something was wrong with his health?
options: Feeling hungry before meals
Being unable to sleep well
Wanting a holiday
Disliking public speaking
quiz.explanation: He watched for small signs like poor sleep and consulted a good physician if something seemed weak.

cards.title: Sleep on emotional decisions and talk them over first
cards.body:
Washington's rule was to finish each day's work before leaving it, with one exception. When a decision was especially hard and stirred strong emotions, he waited: he slept on it, or discussed it first with his wife and friends.

Strong feelings narrow our view and push us toward quick reactions we may regret. A night's sleep lets them settle, and trusted people can point out what we're missing. Speed is valuable for routine matters; for emotionally charged choices, a short pause and a second opinion are often worth more.
cards.quote: I find it a safe rule to sleep over it for a night, or to wait until I have had an opportunity to talk it over with my wife and friends.
cards.locator: XV. The Secret of Success in Public Speaking ¶52
cards.apply_it: If you face an emotional decision now, set it aside until tomorrow and talk it through with one person you trust before acting.

quiz.question: What was the one exception to Washington's rule of finishing each day's work?
options: Letters from donors
Matters involving money
Emotionally difficult decisions, which he slept on
Problems raised by students
quiz.explanation: For hard questions that appealed strongly to the emotions, he waited a night or talked with his wife and friends.

cards.title: Get your hands into the soil to renew your strength
cards.body:
Despite his punishing schedule, Washington made time for his garden at Tuskegee. When he could leave his office early, he would spend thirty or forty minutes digging, planting seeds and tending plants. He wanted contact with real nature, not an imitation, and felt it gave him strength for the hard places waiting in the wider world.

He found similar rest in evening stories and Sunday walks in the woods with his wife and children. Time outdoors, especially working with living things, can be a simple, low-cost way to recover from stress and return to work with a clearer mind.
cards.quote: I pity the man or woman who has never learned to enjoy nature and to get strength and inspiration out of it.
cards.locator: XV. The Secret of Success in Public Speaking ¶56
cards.apply_it: Spend twenty minutes this week tending a plant, garden or green space with your hands, and notice how you feel afterwards.

quiz.question: How did Washington use his garden?
options: As a source of rest, strength and inspiration
Mainly to grow crops for sale
As a place to hold staff meetings
He had no time for a garden
quiz.explanation: He spent thirty or forty minutes digging and planting when he could, finding strength for his duties.

cards.title: Use fame and money as tools for doing good
cards.body:
By the end of his autobiography, Washington had become one of the best-known Americans of his day. He said he had never sought fame for its own sake and valued it only as a means of doing good, just as wealth can be.

He noticed that some of the wealthy donors he met had the same attitude toward money, and admired the careful way John D. Rockefeller checked that each gift would do the most good. Whatever influence or money you gain, large or small, the question he poses is: what useful thing will I do with it?
cards.quote: I have always looked upon fame as something to be used in accomplishing good.
cards.locator: XVII. Last Words ¶10
cards.apply_it: Name one form of influence you have, such as a following, a title or savings. Choose one way to use it for someone else's good this month.

quiz.question: How did Washington regard the fame that came to him?
options: As a reward he had long sought
As a burden he tried to escape
As a way to grow his personal fortune
As something to be used for doing good
quiz.explanation: He said he never sought fame and valued it only as an instrument for doing good, just as wealth may be.
